_about: One example per ability of the strands decider (sources: the strands-decider README and docs/vision.md). `measured` blocks were recorded through app.answer() on the stated model and date -- never typed by hand.

families.label: Pick
families.blurb: choice: one of N options, each with a probability, plus a confidence

families.label: Rate
families.blurb: score: an ordered rubric read as an expected value

families.label: Yes-No
families.blurb: noul: P(true) -- with two outcomes the probability is the uncertainty

families.label: Agentic
families.blurb: the decisions inside an agent loop: routing, tool checks, guardrails, rules

families.label: Vision
families.blurb: questions over pixels -- Qwen3.5 models only, the Gemma 4 deciders read text

families.label: Code
families.blurb: yes/no over a short function (v1: 0.836 on held-out code tasks, README)

examples.title: triage choice
examples.shows: The README's triage example: route one support message to the team that should own it.
examples.teaches: A choice answer is a distribution over the options, not a label: billing wins, but 23% of the mass sits elsewhere, and the confidence (0.659) is the thing you act on, not the argmax.
examples.state: Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days!
examples.expected_shape: choice -> billing (confidence ~0.659); billing ~0.773, sales ~0.121, retail ~0.106 (README, cpu)

examples.title: urgency yes/no
examples.shows: The README's noul example: is this message urgent?
examples.teaches: noul returns P(true) and nothing else -- there is no separate confidence field because with two outcomes the probability already IS the uncertainty. Closer to 1 leans yes.
examples.state: Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days!

examples.title: frustration score
examples.shows: The README's score example: rate the writer on an ordered rubric calm < frustrated < depressed.
examples.teaches: A score is the expected value over ordered levels (1.03 sits just past 'frustrated' at index 1), so the levels you type ARE the scale; the per-level probabilities show where the mass actually sits.
examples.state: Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days!

examples.title: three questions, one read
examples.shows: All three README questions on the same state in one request -- the state is encoded once and each question adds only its own tokens.
examples.teaches: Many questions about one text are nearly free: the usage line shows the input tokens for the whole request, and the three answers are identical to asking them one at a time.
examples.state: Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days!
examples.expected_shape: noul ~0.858 · choice billing (~0.659) · score ~1.03 -- the same numbers as the three single-question examples

examples.title: model routing
examples.shows: Pick the LLM for a task: a small fast model or a large careful one (README: 'Model routing -- pick the right LLM for a task').
examples.teaches: The options are defined by the request, not baked into the weights -- rename them to your own model tiers and the head still scores each by its own last token.
examples.state: User request: "Draft a 3-page legal memo comparing the indemnification clauses in these two vendor contracts and flag any asymmetric liability caps."

questions.instructions: Which model should handle this request?

examples.expected_shape: choice -> one of the two tiers, with P(each) and a confidence

examples.title: argument check
examples.shows: A tool call as the state; verify it before it runs (README: 'Argument checking -- verify a tool call's arguments before it runs').
examples.teaches: Structured text is fine as state -- JSON goes in as-is. Gate the call on P(true) with a threshold you choose; below it, ask the user instead of guessing.
examples.state:
Tool: send_email(to, subject, body)
Call: {"to": "", "subject": "Q3 invoice", "body": "Hi, attached is the Q3 invoice. Best, Sam"}

questions.instructions: Are the arguments complete and ready to execute?

examples.expected_shape: noul P(true) -- low, since `to` is empty

examples.title: grounding check
examples.shows: A guardrail: is a claim supported by the passage it cites? (README: 'Guardrails -- grounding checks').
examples.teaches: The same noul primitive is a hallucination detector when the state holds both the evidence and the claim; the decider reads them together in one pass, no generation.
examples.state:
Passage: The clinic opens at 8:00 on weekdays and 9:00 on Saturdays. It is closed on Sundays and public holidays.
Claim: The clinic is open on Sundays from 9:00.

questions.instructions: Is the claim supported by the passage?

examples.expected_shape: noul P(true) -- low: the passage says closed on Sundays

examples.title: apply a policy
examples.shows: A short written policy plus a case; choose the outcome the policy dictates (v1 trained on rule-application rows -- README 'About the model').
examples.teaches: Decision models apply rules you write in plain words at request time; there is nothing to retrain when the policy changes -- edit the state.
examples.state:
Policy: Refunds are approved automatically within 14 days of purchase. Between 15 and 30 days a refund needs a manager's approval. After 30 days refunds are denied unless the item arrived defective.
Case: Purchased 22 days ago, item works, customer changed their mind.

questions.instructions: What does the policy say should happen?

examples.expected_shape: choice -> needs manager approval (22 days falls in the 15-30 band)

examples.title: language id
examples.shows: The README's example: which language is 'sihamba ngokushesha' in?
examples.teaches: Options can be anything nameable: the head compares the <answer> hidden state against each option's own last token, so a label set of languages works like a label set of teams.

questions.instructions: What language is this phrase in?

examples.title: judge an answer
examples.shows: Evaluation as a decision: score a model's answer against a rubric from 0 to 4 (README: 'Evaluations -- score model outputs').
examples.teaches: An ordered rubric turns the decider into a cheap judge: the expected value is a continuous grade and the per-level mass tells you how sure it is of that grade.
examples.state:
Question: What is the capital of Australia?
Model answer: The capital of Australia is Sydney, its largest city.
Rubric: 4 = correct and complete, 3 = correct with a minor flaw, 2 = partly correct, 1 = mostly wrong, 0 = wrong or no answer.

questions.instructions: Grade the model answer against the rubric.

examples.expected_shape: score near the low end (Canberra is the capital)

examples.title: signature: filled
examples.shows: The README's vision example on a form WE drew: a release form whose signature block carries a signature and a date.
examples.teaches: The image is encoded into the state as vision tokens, so the question, the readout and the confidence are the text model's; nothing was trained on images. Qwen3.5 models only -- Gemma 4 deciders drop the vision encoder.

questions.instructions: Is the signature block filled in?

examples.expected_shape: noul P(true) -- higher than on the empty form

examples.title: signature: empty
examples.shows: The same form with the signature block left empty -- the control for the example above.
examples.teaches: Compare the two P(true) values: the difference between them is what the model reads from the pixels. Small differences mean 'not sure' -- that is the calibration doing its job.

questions.instructions: Is the signature block filled in?

examples.expected_shape: noul P(true) -- lower than on the signed form

examples.title: which shape
examples.shows: A choice over pixels: one large shape is drawn; pick which.
examples.teaches: choice works over images exactly as over text -- per-option probabilities and a confidence -- because the option tokens are text appended after the image.

questions.instructions: Which shape is drawn in the image?

examples.title: empty list?
examples.shows: A short Python function; does it handle the empty list? (v1 answers code questions: 0.836 on 1,996 held-out code tasks, README.)
examples.teaches: Code is just state. One forward pass answers a property of the function, which is what an agent needs before it runs or merges something -- faster than asking an LLM to explain.

questions.instructions: Does this function handle the empty list?

examples.expected_shape: noul P(true) -- low: len([]) == 0 divides by zero
